title: Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Linear Regression: A Proof of Concept via Variational Hamiltonian Formulation
abstract_summary: This preprint presents a theoretical proof-of-concept for variational quantum linear regression by encoding regression weights as Pauli-Z expectation values and reformulating the squared loss as an explicit quantum Hamiltonian. The framework provides explicit matrix constructions, parameter-shift gradient rules, convergence analysis for quantum gradient descent, and argues that the encoding induces natural bounded regularization suitable for NISQ devices, with potential applications to financial time series forecasting (e.g., Thai SET Index).
methodology_description: The paper develops a rigorous theoretical mapping of classical linear regression into a variational quantum optimization problem. Weights are encoded as expectation values of Pauli-Z operators on individual qubits (wj = ⟨Zj⟩), using a product-state Ry(θ) ansatz |ψ(θ)⟩ = ⊗j Ry(θj)|0⟩ so that wj = cos(θj). For each data point (xi, yi) the squared loss is written as the expectation value of an explicitly constructed Hamiltonian ˆHi = αi I − βi ∑j xij Zj + γi ∑j,k xij xik ZjZk (with given coefficients), and the total loss is L(θ) = (1/N) ∑i ⟨ψ(θ)|ˆHi|ψ(θ)⟩ + λR(θ). The approach provides full matrix representations for small d and algorithms for constructing d-qubit Hamiltonians and for efficient expectation computation (reducing complexity to O(d^2) per evaluation using cos(θj) evaluations). Gradients are computed with the parameter-shift rule and used in a classical outer-loop gradient descent optimizer (Algorithm 1: Variational Quantum Linear Regression). The methodology includes analysis of measurement and gate noise, shot complexity (M = O(1/ϵ^2)), convergence proofs under Lipschitz/smoothness assumptions (O(1/√K) rate), and a theoretical characterization of induced regularization (implicit bound wj ∈ [−1,1] and Rimplicit(θ) = ∑ sin^2(θj/2)). The paper provides explicit pseudocode for Hamiltonian construction and expectation evaluation, complexity accounting for circuit depth and measurement overhead, and a proposed implementation plan (Qiskit/Aer simulations with realistic noise models and optional IBM hardware access). Feature-scaling and preprocessing for financial data (scaling features to [−1,1], truncation of targets) and an intended application to SET Index forecasting (Yahoo Finance SET.BK daily data, 2020–2025) are described as a future empirical validation rather than executed experiments.
dataset_used: Proposed dataset: Yahoo Finance historical Thai SET Index (ticker SET.BK), daily data for 2020–2025, with possible supplementary features (USD/THB exchange rates, bond yields, regional indices). Features proposed include returns, moving averages, realized volatility, RSI, MACD, normalized volume, VWAP; target is truncated signed next-day return.
key_findings: [speculative] Introduces a complete mathematical mapping from classical linear regression to a variational quantum formulation by encoding weights as Pauli-Z expectation values (wj = ⟨Zj⟩ = cos θj).
[speculative] Presents an explicit Hamiltonian formulation of the squared loss for each data point: ˆHi = αi I − βi Σj xij Zj + γi Σj,k xijxik ZjZk, with explicit matrix representations for small d.
[speculative] Proposes a NISQ-compatible variational algorithm for linear regression using shallow Ry rotations (O(d) gates) and the parameter-shift rule for gradient estimation.
[speculative] Claims natural/implicit regularization arises from the encoding since weights are constrained to [−1, 1], with an explicit implicit regularizer Rimplicit(θ) = Σj sin^2(θj/2).

[speculative] Derives a Riemannian metric on parameter space induced by the encoding (gjk(θ) = sin^2(θj) δjk) and analyzes geometric consequences (degeneracy at θj = 0, π, variable effective step sizes).
[speculative] Provides a theoretical convergence analysis for quantum gradient descent under bounded gradients/Lipschitz continuity, claiming convergence to stationary points at rate O(1/√K).

[speculative] Gives complexity estimates for the variational approach: circuit preparation O(d), gradient estimation requiring O(2 d M) measurements per iteration using parameter shifts, and measurement-shot scaling M = O(1/ε^2).

[speculative] States that when the classical optimal weights lie within [−1,1] (∞-norm ≤ 1), the quantum variational solution can match the classical loss; otherwise the quantum solution is the best constrained approximation (error bound claimed).

[speculative] Asserts practical advantages in constrained optimization and financial modeling (e.g., naturally bounded weights aligning with position limits), and outlines a pipeline for applying the method to SET Index forecasting using Yahoo Finance data.

[speculative] Provides error/noise analysis: statistical measurement error σstat = sqrt((1 − ⟨Z⟩^2)/M) and models gate depolarizing noise and coherence effects, with a claimed noise-resilient (but degraded) convergence bound.

[speculative] Supplies explicit algorithms for Hamiltonian matrix construction and efficient expectation-value computation reducing naive 2^d costs to O(d^2) arithmetic for classical evaluation of the expectation formula.

[speculative] Positions the approach as mathematically complete and NISQ-implementable in contrast to HHL-style fault-tolerant algorithms, claiming practical implementability rather than exponential speedup.
results_summary: This preprint develops a theoretical variational quantum formulation of linear regression by encoding each regression weight as the Pauli-Z expectation of a qubit (wj = cos θj), constructing explicit Hamiltonians whose expectation values equal squared-loss terms, and proposing a NISQ-friendly optimization pipeline using Ry rotations and the parameter-shift rule. The paper derives geometric properties of the induced parameter manifold, an implicit regularizer arising from the bounded encoding, complexity estimates for circuit and measurement costs, convergence guarantees under standard smoothness assumptions (O(1/√K)), and noise/error scaling relations. It frames potential applications to financial forecasting (e.g., SET Index) and supplies matrix- and algorithm-level constructions intended to enable implementation on current quantum hardware or simulators. Most claims are theoretical derivations and proposals rather than empirical demonstrations.
performance_claims: Circuit preparation: O(d) quantum gates per evaluation (claimed).
Measurement-shot scaling: M = O(1/ε^2) to achieve precision ε on expectation values (claimed).
Gradient computation measurements: O(2 d M) per iteration using parameter-shift rule (claimed).
Total quantum complexity (per K iterations): O(K N d M) measurements/evaluations (claimed).
Convergence rate for quantum gradient descent: O(1/√K) to a stationary point under bounded gradients and Lipschitz continuity (claimed).
Expectation-value statistical error: σstat = sqrt((1 − ⟨Z⟩^2)/M) leading to loss error bound σloss ≤ ||x||^2 sqrt(d/M) (claimed).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper does not present empirical demonstrations of quantum advantage; it makes theoretical/speculative claims that the variational encoding offers advantages in constrained optimization and 'natural' regularization for NISQ devices (bounded weights, altered optimization geometry) rather than asymptotic exponential speedups. The asserted benefits are analytical/theoretical and intended as a proof-of-concept for NISQ applicability rather than demonstrated performance gains.
limitations: Requires measurement-heavy evaluation: gradient estimation via parameter-shift needs O(2dM) measurements per iteration and M = O(1/ϵ^2) shots for precision (author-stated).

Weights are intrinsically constrained to [−1, 1] by the encoding; if classical optimal weights lie outside this range the method only provides the best constrained approximation (author-stated, Proposition 8.3).
No empirical validation provided — all results are theoretical/proof-of-concept (author-stated).

Explicit Hamiltonian matrices and full state representations are 2^d × 2^d objects; direct manipulation scales exponentially in qubit count (author-stated that direct matrix-vector multiplication is prohibitive; scalability limits not resolved).
Noise sensitivity: measurement statistical error, gate infidelity (depolarizing noise), and finite coherence time degrade performance and introduce bias (author-stated, Sec. 12).
Convergence guarantees are to stationary points for a non-convex objective with rate O(1/√K); no guarantee of global optimality (author-stated, Sec. 8.1).
The approach does not claim exponential quantum speedup; complexity improvements are polynomial/practical only (author-stated comparisons with HHL approaches).
[inferred] The ansatz used (product of single-qubit Ry rotations) limits expressivity/representational power compared with entangling circuits — potential underfitting for complex data.
[inferred] Barren-plateau and trainability issues are not addressed in the proofs or algorithmic design, despite being known problems for variational circuits.
[inferred] Several theoretical results assume bounded gradients and Lipschitz continuity; these assumptions may not hold in realistic, noisy hardware or with richer ansätze.
[inferred] The claimed "natural regularization" via bounded weights is qualitatively different from L2 but its practical tuning/efficacy across datasets is not quantified empirically.
[inferred] Construction of per-data-point Hamiltonians (one Hamiltonian per training example) may be computationally and memory intensive for large N.
[inferred] The constants in approximation/error bounds (e.g., the C in Proposition 8.3) are unspecified and dataset-dependent, limiting practical interpretability of theoretical guarantees.

[inferred] The mapping/equivalence statements to classical regression complexity are asserted at a high level but lack rigorous complexity-theoretic proofs comparing resource costs in realistic settings (shots, noise, circuit depth).
